sections.heading: What does voice tell us?
sections.text: Voice tells us whether the subject performs an action or receives it. In active voice, the subject is the doer: “Ram writes a letter.” Ram is the subject, writes is the verb, and a letter is the object. In passive voice, the receiver becomes the focus: “A letter is written by Ram.” The meaning is similar, but the emphasis changes.

sections.heading: The basic formula
sections.text: To change an active sentence into passive, move its object to the front, use a suitable helping verb, and put the main verb in its third form (V3). Add “by” + the doer when that information matters. Active: Subject + Verb + Object. Passive: Object + Helping verb + V3 + (by + subject). V3 means the past participle, such as written, eaten, done, or taken.

sections.heading: A step-by-step method
sections.text: Take “The teacher checks the answers.” First identify the object: “the answers.” Move it to the front. The verb is simple present, so use is/are + V3; “answers” is plural, so choose “are.” The passive sentence is “The answers are checked by the teacher.” Keep the tense, match the helping verb to the new subject, and include the doer only if useful.

sections.heading: Pronouns after “by”
sections.text: When a subject pronoun moves after “by,” use its object form: I → me, we → us, he → him, she → her, they → them, and who → whom. For example, “She helped him” becomes “He was helped by her.”

sections.heading: When is passive voice useful?
sections.text: Use passive when the receiver of the action is more important than the doer, or when the doer is unknown or unimportant. “The road was repaired yesterday” is clear even if we do not know who repaired it. In this case, the by-phrase can be left out.

sections.heading: When can a sentence not become passive?
sections.text: A passive form normally needs an object to move into the subject position. So, sentences with a transitive verb (a verb that takes an object) can usually change voice: “She opened the door” → “The door was opened by her.” An intransitive verb has no object, so “The baby slept” cannot normally be changed into passive voice.

voiceExamples.passive: Cricket is being played by him.
The work has been completed by them.
A letter was written by Ram.
A car will be bought by her.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The work is do by him.
commonMistakes.correct: The work is done by him.

commonMistakes.incorrect: A letter was wrote by Ram.
commonMistakes.correct: A letter was written by Ram.
Food is being cooked by her.

quiz.question: The teacher praised the student. Choose the passive voice.
options: The student praised the teacher.
The student was praised by the teacher.
The student is praised by the teacher.
The teacher was praised by the student.
quiz.explanation: “Praised” is simple past, so use was/were + V3. The singular object “the student” becomes the new subject.

quiz.question: She is reading a book. Choose the passive voice.
options: A book is read by her.
A book was being read by her.
A book is being read by her.
A book has been read by her.
quiz.explanation: The active verb is present continuous. Its passive form is is/am/are + being + V3.

quiz.question: They have finished the project. Choose the passive voice.
options: The project had been finished by them.
The project has been finished by them.
The project is finished by them.
The project was finished by them.
quiz.explanation: The active verb is present perfect. Use has/have + been + V3; “project” is singular, so use “has.”

quiz.question: Choose the correct passive form: “Someone stole my phone.”
options: My phone is stolen.
My phone was stolen.
My phone has stole.
My phone had steal.
quiz.explanation: “Stole” is simple past. “My phone” is singular, so the passive is “was stolen.” The unknown doer can be omitted.

quiz.question: Which sentence cannot normally be changed into passive voice?
options: She opened the door.
He kicked the ball.
The baby slept.
They built a house.
quiz.explanation: “Slept” has no object. Without an object to move into the subject position, the sentence cannot normally be made passive.

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: An adjective describes or limits a noun or pronoun: a careful driver, a blue bag, she is confident.

sections.heading: Kinds
sections.text: Quality (honest), quantity (some), number (three), demonstrative (this), possessive (my), interrogative (which), distributive (each), and proper adjectives (Indian).

sections.heading: Order
sections.text: When several adjectives occur together, a common order is opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose + noun: a lovely small old round red Italian wooden box.

sections.heading: Degrees
sections.text: Positive: tall. Comparative: taller. Superlative: tallest. Longer adjectives often use more/most. Irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst.

sections.heading: Comparison rules
sections.text: Use than with a comparative: “older than”. Use the with a superlative: “the tallest”. Avoid double comparison: “more better” is incorrect.

sections.heading: Participial adjectives
sections.text: -ing often describes the source of a feeling (boring); -ed often describes the person experiencing it (bored): “The lecture was boring; I was bored.”

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, another adverb, or a whole clause: speaks clearly, very tall, quite slowly, fortunately.

sections.heading: Kinds
sections.text: Manner (carefully), place (here), time (yesterday), frequency (often), degree (very), and sentence adverbs (fortunately).

sections.heading: Position
sections.text: Adverbs of frequency usually come before the main verb but after be: “She often reads”; “She is always punctual.”

sections.heading: Formation
sections.text: Many adverbs use -ly (quick → quickly), but not all: fast, hard, late, well. Some -ly words are adjectives (friendly, lovely).

sections.heading: Adjective or adverb
sections.text: Use an adjective after linking verbs such as look, feel, seem: “The soup tastes good.” Use an adverb to modify an action: “She sings well.”

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.text: Hard means with effort; hardly means almost not. Late means not on time; lately means recently.

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: A synonym has a similar meaning; an antonym has an opposite meaning. Exact equivalence is rare, so context matters.

sections.heading: Synonym examples
sections.text: Abundant: plentiful. Brief: concise. Candid: frank. Diligent: hardworking. Reluctant: unwilling. Vivid: striking or clear.

sections.heading: Antonym examples
sections.text: Ancient ↔ modern. Expand ↔ contract. Generous ↔ stingy. Hostile ↔ friendly. Scarce ↔ abundant. Transparent ↔ opaque.

sections.heading: Context matters
sections.text: “Bright” may mean shining, intelligent, or vivid. Select the meaning that fits the sentence rather than memorising one substitute.

sections.heading: Word strength and tone
sections.text: Slim and skinny are related but differ in tone. Examine formality, emotion and intensity when choosing a synonym.

sections.heading: Exam approach
sections.text: Read the complete sentence, substitute the option, and test whether grammar, meaning and tone remain appropriate.

sections.heading: The three articles
sections.text: A, an and the are articles. A/an are indefinite; the is definite.

sections.heading: A or an
sections.text: Use a before a consonant sound (a university, a book) and an before a vowel sound (an hour, an apple). Choose by sound, not spelling.

sections.heading: The
sections.text: Use the for something identified or specific, something already mentioned, unique things in context, and many names of rivers, seas, mountain ranges and groups of islands.

sections.heading: No article
sections.text: Use no article for plural or uncountable nouns when speaking generally: “Books are useful”; “Water is essential.”

sections.heading: Common patterns
sections.text: Use a/an for professions: “She is an engineer.” Use the when a noun is made specific: “The book on the desk is mine.”

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.text: Incorrect: “He is an university student.” Correct: “He is a university student.” Incorrect: “The honesty is important.” Usually: “Honesty is important.”

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: A cloze test is a passage with selected words removed. You choose the word that best completes each gap.

sections.heading: Read the whole passage
sections.text: Read once before filling gaps. Identify topic, tense, point of view and overall tone.

sections.heading: Grammar clues
sections.text: Check subject–verb agreement, tense, articles, prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions and singular/plural forms.

sections.heading: Meaning clues
sections.text: Use context, collocations and logical links. A grammatically possible word may still be wrong if it does not fit the meaning.

sections.heading: Linking words
sections.text: Notice contrast (however, although), cause (because, therefore), addition (moreover), and sequence (first, finally).

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Fill easy blanks first, reread the completed sentence and then the full paragraph, and ensure every choice fits both grammar and meaning.

sections.heading: Study method
sections.text: Learn spelling in context. Break long words into syllables, notice repeated letter patterns, and keep a personal list of words you often misspell.

sections.heading: Frequently confused
sections.text: accommodate (double c, double m); necessary (one c, double s); separate (not seperate); definitely (not definately); environment; government; occurrence (double c, double r); privilege.

sections.heading: More useful spellings
sections.text: receive; believe; achieve; maintenance; embarrass; questionnaire; pronunciation; beginning; committee; recommend; calendar; conscience.

sections.heading: Common patterns
sections.text: “i before e” is only a rough guide and has exceptions. Watch silent letters (debt, doubt), doubled consonants (beginning), and suffix changes (happy → happiness).

sections.heading: Proofreading routine
sections.text: Read slowly, check endings and doubled letters, use a dictionary for uncertain words, and proofread once for meaning and once only for spelling.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.text: Choose the correct spelling: accommodate / accomodate; separate / seperate; definitely / definately; privilege / priviledge. Answers: accommodate, separate, definitely, privilege.

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: An idiom is a fixed expression whose overall meaning may not be obvious from the individual words.

sections.heading: Everyday examples
sections.text: A piece of cake = very easy; once in a blue moon = very rarely; break the ice = ease social tension; hit the nail on the head = say exactly the right thing.

sections.heading: More examples
sections.text: Under the weather = feeling unwell; spill the beans = reveal a secret; cost an arm and a leg = be very expensive; call it a day = stop working for now.

sections.heading: Use in context
sections.text: Choose an idiom only when its meaning and tone fit the situation. Avoid forcing idioms into formal writing.

sections.heading: Exam approach
sections.text: Read the whole sentence, identify the situation, replace the idiom with a plain meaning, and check whether the sentence still makes sense.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.text: “The test was a piece of cake.” Meaning: the test was very easy.

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: Direct speech quotes the speaker's exact words: He said, “I am tired.” Indirect speech reports the meaning without quotation marks: He said that he was tired.

sections.heading: Pronouns and time
sections.text: Pronouns change according to the speaker and listener. Depending on the reporting context, now may become then, today that day, tomorrow the next day, and yesterday the previous day.

sections.heading: Backshift
sections.text: When the reporting verb is in the past, present simple often changes to past simple, present continuous to past continuous, and will to would. A fact that remains universally true may keep its present tense.

sections.heading: Statements
sections.text: Use said (that) or told + object (that): “She said that she was ready.” / “She told me that she was ready.”

sections.heading: Questions and commands
sections.text: Reported questions use statement word order: “He asked where I lived.” Commands use told/asked + object + to-infinitive: “She told me to wait.”

sections.heading: Punctuation
sections.text: Direct speech uses quotation marks and appropriate punctuation. Indirect speech does not use quotation marks around the reported words.

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: A noun names a person, place, animal, thing, substance, or idea. Examples: teacher, Delhi, tiger, pencil, water, honesty.

sections.heading: Main types
sections.text: Proper: a particular name (Aarav, India). Common: a general name (student, city). Collective: a group (team, flock). Material: a substance (gold, cotton). Abstract: an idea or quality (kindness, courage).

sections.heading: Number
sections.text: Singular names one (book); plural names more than one (books). Common patterns: add -s/-es; consonant + y becomes -ies (city → cities); some forms are irregular (child → children, mouse → mice).

sections.heading: Gender
sections.text: English nouns may refer to masculine, feminine, common, or neuter gender. Examples: king/queen; teacher (common); table (neuter).

sections.heading: Countable and uncountable
sections.text: Countable nouns take numbers and a/an (an apple, three apples). Uncountable nouns usually do not (advice, furniture, information); say a piece of advice.

sections.heading: Quick check
sections.text: Identify the nouns: “The brave girl carried a basket of flowers.” Nouns: girl, basket, flowers. “Honesty builds trust.” Abstract nouns: honesty, trust.

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: A one-word substitution replaces a phrase or description with one precise word.

sections.heading: People and beliefs
sections.text: Atheist: a person who does not believe in a god or gods. Optimist: one who expects favourable outcomes. Pessimist: one who expects unfavourable outcomes. Orphan: a child whose parents have died.

sections.heading: Knowledge and language
sections.text: Bilingual: using two languages. Polyglot: knowing or using several languages. Autobiography: a person's account of their own life. Biography: an account of another person's life.

sections.heading: Places and collections
sections.text: Aquarium: a place/tank for aquatic animals. Library: a collection/place for books. Museum: a place where objects of historical, artistic or scientific interest are kept.

sections.heading: Common distinctions
sections.text: Anonymous = of unknown identity; illegible = impossible or difficult to read; invincible = unable to be defeated; inevitable = certain to happen.

sections.heading: Exam approach
sections.text: Underline the defining feature in the phrase, eliminate near-synonyms, and check the word's part of speech before choosing.

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: A parajumble gives sentences in a mixed order. Arrange them so they form a logical and coherent paragraph.

sections.heading: Find the opening
sections.text: Look for a sentence that introduces the topic without depending on an earlier reference. Definitions and broad introductions often open a paragraph.

sections.heading: Pronoun links
sections.text: A sentence beginning with he, she, it, they, this or these usually refers to something already introduced.

sections.heading: Connectors and sequence
sections.text: Words such as however, therefore, then, finally and for example signal relationships. Dates, stages and cause-effect links can reveal order.

sections.heading: Build pairs
sections.text: Find sentences that clearly belong together, such as a general statement followed by an example or a claim followed by its explanation.

sections.heading: Final check
sections.text: Read the proposed paragraph from start to finish. It should have a clear opening, connected development and a sensible conclusion.

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: A phrasal verb combines a verb with an adverb or preposition (or both) to create a meaning: give up, look after, put up with.

sections.heading: Common examples
sections.text: Give up = stop trying; look after = take care of; find out = discover; carry on = continue; put off = postpone.

sections.heading: More examples
sections.text: Turn down = reject; bring up = mention/raise; run into = meet unexpectedly; set up = arrange or establish; call off = cancel.

sections.heading: Separable forms
sections.text: Some phrasal verbs can be separated: “turn the offer down” / “turn down the offer”. With a pronoun, separation is required: “turn it down”.

sections.heading: Inseparable forms
sections.text: Some cannot be separated: “look after the child”, not “look the child after”. Learn the verb and particle together.

sections.heading: Exam approach
sections.text: Use the surrounding sentence to infer meaning. Check whether the object is required and whether the particle can move.

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: A preposition shows a relationship of place, time, direction, cause, or manner: in the room, at noon, towards home, because of rain.

sections.heading: Place
sections.text: At often marks a point (at the gate); in an enclosed area (in the room); on a surface (on the table).

sections.heading: Time
sections.text: At: clock time (at 6 pm). On: days/dates (on Monday). In: months, years and longer periods (in July, in 2026).

sections.heading: Movement
sections.text: To indicates destination; into indicates movement from outside to inside; onto indicates movement to a surface; through indicates movement within and out of something.

sections.heading: Common combinations
sections.text: Interested in, good at, depend on, afraid of, responsible for, listen to, belong to. Learn these as word partnerships.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.text: Say “arrive at the station” and “arrive in Delhi”; “different from” is widely accepted. Avoid adding an unnecessary preposition after discuss: “discuss the issue”.

sections.heading: Meaning
sections.text: A pronoun replaces a noun or noun phrase to avoid repetition: “Mira is kind. She helps others.”

sections.heading: Personal pronouns
sections.text: Subject forms: I, we, you, he, she, it, they. Object forms: me, us, you, him, her, it, them. Example: They invited us.

sections.heading: Possessive forms
sections.text: Possessive determiners come before nouns (my book, their house). Possessive pronouns stand alone (mine, yours, hers, ours, theirs).

sections.heading: Reflexive and emphatic
sections.text: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves. Reflexive: “She blamed herself.” Emphatic: “The principal herself spoke.”

sections.heading: Other types
sections.text: Demonstrative: this, that, these, those. Interrogative: who, whom, whose, which, what. Relative: who, whom, whose, which, that. Indefinite: someone, anybody, few, many. Reciprocal: each other, one another.

sections.heading: Agreement
sections.text: A pronoun should agree with its antecedent in person and number. Keep the reference clear: “When Riya met Neha, she smiled” is ambiguous; name the person if needed.

sections.heading: Meaning and form
sections.text: A question tag is a short question added to a statement: “You are ready, aren’t you?”

sections.heading: Positive and negative
sections.text: Positive statement usually takes a negative tag; negative statement usually takes a positive tag: “She can swim, can’t she?” / “He isn’t late, is he?”

sections.heading: Auxiliary verbs
sections.text: Repeat the auxiliary or modal in the tag. If there is no auxiliary in the simple present/past, use do/does/did.

sections.heading: Special patterns
sections.text: “I am” → “aren’t I?”; “Let’s…” → “shall we?”; imperative requests often use “will you?”; “There is…” → “isn’t there?”

sections.heading: Indefinite subjects
sections.text: Words such as everyone, somebody and nobody usually take they in modern standard tags: “Everyone has arrived, haven’t they?”

sections.heading: Punctuation
sections.text: Separate the statement and tag with a comma; finish with a question mark.

sections.heading: Practice passage
sections.text: Public parks are more than attractive open spaces. They provide room for exercise, quiet recreation and informal meetings. In crowded cities, trees can offer shade and help soften the effects of heat. Parks also give children a place to play and allow neighbours to meet beyond the walls of their homes.

sections.heading: Main idea
sections.text: The passage explains the social, recreational and environmental value of urban parks.

sections.heading: Detail questions
sections.text: According to the passage, parks provide space for exercise, quiet recreation and informal meetings. Trees can offer shade and help reduce the effects of heat.

sections.heading: Inference
sections.text: The passage suggests that parks can strengthen neighbourhood connections because they create shared public spaces.

sections.heading: Vocabulary in context
sections.text: “Informal” means relaxed or not highly structured in this context.

sections.heading: Practice questions
sections.text: 1. What is the central idea? 2. Name two benefits of trees in parks mentioned or implied. 3. Why might parks help neighbours connect? 4. What does “informal” mean here?

sections.heading: Answer guide
sections.text: 1. Parks benefit city life in several ways. 2. They provide shade and help soften urban heat. 3. They offer shared places for people to meet. 4. Relaxed or not highly structured.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: Reading comprehension tests whether you can understand a passage, identify its central idea, infer meaning, and distinguish evidence from opinion.

sections.heading: First reading
sections.text: Read the passage once for its overall subject, purpose and tone. Notice repeated ideas, contrast words and the author's conclusion.

sections.heading: Question types
sections.text: Main idea, specific detail, inference, vocabulary in context, tone, purpose, title, and statements supported or not supported by the passage.

sections.heading: Evidence-based answers
sections.text: Return to the relevant lines. Choose the option supported by the passage, not merely one that sounds reasonable from outside knowledge.

sections.heading: Inference and tone
sections.text: An inference must follow from clues in the text. Tone may be critical, optimistic, sceptical, neutral, persuasive, humorous or reflective.

sections.heading: Time strategy
sections.text: Read the question carefully, locate relevant information, eliminate extreme or unsupported options, and avoid spending too long on one question.

sections.heading: What tense shows
sections.text: Tense locates an action or state in time. English commonly teaches present, past and future, each with simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous forms.

sections.heading: Present forms
sections.text: Simple: I study. Continuous: I am studying. Perfect: I have studied. Perfect continuous: I have been studying for an hour.

sections.heading: Past forms
sections.text: Simple: I studied. Continuous: I was studying. Perfect: I had studied before dinner. Perfect continuous: I had been studying for an hour before dinner.

sections.heading: Future forms
sections.text: Simple: I will study. Continuous: I will be studying at 8. Perfect: I will have studied by 8. Perfect continuous: By 8, I will have been studying for two hours.

sections.heading: Use and clues
sections.text: Simple present: habits/facts. Present continuous: action happening now or temporary situation. Present perfect: past action linked to now. Present perfect continuous: duration continuing to now. Use since for a starting point and for for a period.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.text: Use the base verb after do/does/did: “Did she go?” not “Did she went?” Avoid stative verbs in continuous forms in ordinary use: “I know”, not usually “I am knowing”.
